---
name: tarea1-mcp-infra
description: IIC3103 Tarea 1 IntegraTrip — course-provided AS + MCP server endpoints and their OAuth mechanisms
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: project
  originSessionId: 9bb83558-22a6-4ad1-a92b-951c18461074
---

IntegraTrip = MCP client for IIC3103 Tarea 1. Course-provided infra (probed 2026-09-04):

- Auth Server (AS): `https://tarea1-auth-z2fqxmm2ja-uc.a.run.app` — custom Express app (NOT real Keycloak) that mimics realm URLs. RS256 JWTs, one shared JWKS at `/.well-known/jwks.json`. Users pre-registered with email + student number as password; AS dashboard lets you create OAuth clients.
- MCP servers (Streamable HTTP at `/mcp`, scope `mcp:tools`):
  - PRE (Andes Air, flights): `https://tarea1-mcp-pre-z2fqxmm2ja-uc.a.run.app` → realm `/realms/pre`, Pre-Registered OAuth Client.
  - DCR (StayWell, hotels): `https://tarea1-mcp-dcr-z2fqxmm2ja-uc.a.run.app` → realm `/realms/dcr`, has `registration_endpoint` (RFC 7591 Dynamic Client Registration).
  - CIMD (Cielo Sur, weather): `https://tarea1-mcp-cimd-z2fqxmm2ja-uc.a.run.app` → realm `/realms/cimd`, `client_id_metadata_document_supported:true` (client_id is a hosted HTTPS metadata URL).
- Discovery: unauth POST /mcp → 401 + `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer resource_metadata=".../.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/mcp"`. That PRM lists `authorization_servers:[realm]`, `resource:.../mcp`.
- All realms: `authorization_code`+`refresh_token`, PKCE **S256 required**, `resource_indicators_supported:true` (must send RFC 8707 `resource` param = the `/mcp` URL or token audience fails), token_endpoint_auth_methods `none`|`client_secret_post`, response_types `code`.

Full spec from AS `/docs` (authoritative):
- **App login** (NOT an MCP): realm `pre`, use the pre-registered `/console` client (client_id `pre_…` + client_secret). `resource` = your app ORIGIN (e.g. https://app.com), must equal origin of a registered redirect_uri. Resulting JWT `aud`=origin, has `email`+`student_id`; does NOT work against an MCP. authorize has `prompt=login` to force form.
- **MCP connect** (all 3): `resource` = the MCP `/mcp` URL. authorize params: response_type=code, client_id, redirect_uri (EXACT match), resource, scope=mcp:tools, state, code_challenge, code_challenge_method=S256. token: POST x-www-form-urlencoded grant_type=authorization_code, code, redirect_uri, client_id, code_verifier, resource, client_secret (pre/dcr; OMIT for cimd). Code lives 5 min single-use; access token TTL 3600s; refresh 30 days and ROTATES on use.
- **PRE**: create client in `/console` (name + redirect_uris localhost & prod) → client_id/client_secret. Same client used for login AND Andes Air MCP (differ only by `resource`).
- **DCR**: POST `/realms/dcr/register` JSON {client_name, redirect_uris, grant_types:["authorization_code","refresh_token"], response_types:["code"], token_endpoint_auth_method:"client_secret_post"}; optional `Authorization: Bearer <token>` to own it. → 201 {client_id, client_secret}.
- **CIMD**: client_id = public HTTPS URL of a hosted JSON doc: {client_id:"<same URL>", client_name, redirect_uris:["…/callback"], grant_types:["authorization_code"], response_types:["code"], token_endpoint_auth_method:"none"}. No secret. AS fetches it at authorize time.
- **JWT**: RS256, kid `iic3103-tarea1`, verify vs shared JWKS. Claims: iss(realm), sub(email UC), aud(resource), scope, client_id, email, student_id, iat/exp.
- **AS metadata discovery order**: `/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server{path}` → `{issuer}/.well-known/openid-configuration` → `{issuer}/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server`.
- One `redirect_uri` (`/callback`) serves login + all 3 MCP flows; disambiguate via `state`. Common errors: invalid_target (resource mismatch authorize vs token), redirect_uri not registered (char-exact), invalid_grant (code reused/PKCE fail).

Rubric weights: PRE 10%, DCR 20%, CIMD 20%, tools/list 20%, tools/call 10%, deploy 10%, login 10%. Deploy must stay live 2 weeks for grading. See [[tarea1-plan]].
---
name: tarea1-plan
description: "IntegraTrip Tarea 1 — chosen stack, architecture layout, and build status"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: project
  originSessionId: 9bb83558-22a6-4ad1-a92b-951c18461074
---

**Stack** (approved by user): Next.js 16 App Router + TypeScript monolith (frontend + API in one service), Drizzle ORM + Supabase Postgres, jose (JWT/JWKS), @modelcontextprotocol/sdk (Streamable HTTP), AES-256-GCM for secrets at rest, zod. Deploy target: Render (render.yaml present). Node 22 on Render.

**Layout**:
- `src/config/env.ts` — lazy zod-validated env groups (core/db/crypto/login). Helpers: redirectUri(), clientMetadataDocumentUrl(), loginIssuer(), jwksUrl().
- `src/lib/crypto.ts` — AES-256-GCM encrypt/decrypt + hmac (session).
- `src/lib/db/{schema,index}.ts` — tables: users, mcp_connections, mcp_client_registrations, mcp_tokens, oauth_flows. Migration in /drizzle/0000_init.sql.

# IntegraTrip — Cliente MCP

Cliente [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.info/) para la
Tarea 1 de IIC3103. Permite a un usuario autenticarse, conectar servidores MCP
usando tres mecanismos OAuth distintos, descubrir sus tools (`tools/list`) y
ejecutarlas (`tools/call`) con formularios generados dinámicamente.

## Stack

- **Next.js (App Router) + TypeScript** — monolito que sirve frontend y API.
  Toda la comunicación con credenciales ocurre server-side (Route Handlers).
- **PostgreSQL (Supabase) + Drizzle ORM** — persistencia por usuario.
- **jose** — validación de JWT (RS256) contra el JWKS del AS.
- **@modelcontextprotocol/sdk** — transporte Streamable HTTP hacia los MCP.
- **AES-256-GCM** — cifrado de secretos y tokens en reposo.

## Arquitectura (resumen)

La documentación detallada, incluyendo el modelo entidad-relación y los
diagramas de secuencia de PRE, DCR y CIMD, está en
[docs/architecture.md](./docs/architecture.md).
```
Navegador ──▶ Next.js (Route Handlers = backend server-side)
                 │
                 ├─ Auth de la app: OAuth code+PKCE contra realm `pre`
                 │  (resource = origin de la app), sesión en cookie httpOnly.
                 │
                 ├─ Capa OAuth desacoplada (src/lib/oauth):
                 │    discovery (401→PRM→AS metadata) · PKCE · engine
                 │    (authorize/token/refresh + resource indicator) ·
                 │    providers pre | dcr | cimd  ◀── única variación por mecanismo
                 │
                 ├─ Capa MCP (src/lib/mcp): cliente SDK + tools/list + tools/call
                 │
                 └─ Persistencia (src/lib/db, src/lib/connections):
                      users · mcp_connections · mcp_client_registrations
                      · mcp_tokens · oauth_flows   (secretos/tokens cifrados)
```

Los tres mecanismos comparten **el mismo flujo OAuth 2.1**; sólo difieren en
cómo se obtiene el `client_id`:

| Mecanismo | Servidor  | Cómo se obtiene el client_id                          |
|-----------|-----------|------------------------------------------------------|
| **PRE**   | Andes Air | Cliente pre-registrado en `/console` (id + secret).  |
| **DCR**   | StayWell  | Registro dinámico (RFC 7591) durante la conexión.    |
| **CIMD**  | Cielo Sur | URL HTTPS de un documento de metadata que hospeda la app (`/oauth/client-metadata.json`). Cliente público, sin secret. |

## Desarrollo local

```bash
cp .env.example .env.local   # completa los valores
npm install
npm run db:generate          # (ya versionado en /drizzle)
npm run db:migrate           # aplica el esquema a tu Postgres
npm run dev                  # http://localhost:3000
```

Para OAuth en local necesitas registrar `http://localhost:3000/callback` como
`redirect_uri` en el `/console` del AS, y usar `APP_BASE_URL=http://localhost:3000`.

## Variables de entorno

Ver [`.env.example`](./.env.example). Resumen:

| Variable | Descripción |
|---|---|
| `APP_BASE_URL` | Origin público de la app (= origin del redirect_uri registrado). |
| `AS_BASE_URL` | Servidor de autenticación del curso. |
| `APP_LOGIN_REALM` | Realm de login (`pre`). |
| `DATABASE_URL` | Postgres (Supabase). |
| `ENCRYPTION_KEY` | Clave AES-256-GCM (32 bytes base64) para cifrado en reposo. |
| `SESSION_SECRET` | Firma HMAC de la cookie de sesión. |
| `PRE_CLIENT_ID` / `PRE_CLIENT_SECRET` | Cliente pre-registrado (login + Andes Air). |

- All realms: `authorization_code`+`refresh_token`, PKCE **S256 required**, `resource_indicators_supported:true` (must send RFC 8707 `resource` param = the `/mcp` URL or token audience fails), token_endpoint_auth_methods `none`|`client_secret_post`, response_types `code`.

Full spec from AS `/docs` (authoritative):
- **App login** (NOT an MCP): realm `pre`, use the pre-registered `/console` client (client_id `pre_…` + client_secret). `resource` = your app ORIGIN (e.g. https://app.com), must equal origin of a registered redirect_uri. Resulting JWT `aud`=origin, has `email`+`student_id`; does NOT work against an MCP. authorize has `prompt=login` to force form.
- **MCP connect** (all 3): `resource` = the MCP `/mcp` URL. authorize params: response_type=code, client_id, redirect_uri (EXACT match), resource, scope=mcp:tools, state, code_challenge, code_challenge_method=S256. token: POST x-www-form-urlencoded grant_type=authorization_code, code, redirect_uri, client_id, code_verifier, resource, client_secret (pre/dcr; OMIT for cimd). Code lives 5 min single-use; access token TTL 3600s; refresh 30 days and ROTATES on use.
- **PRE**: create client in `/console` (name + redirect_uris localhost & prod) → client_id/client_secret. Same client used for login AND Andes Air MCP (differ only by `resource`).
- **DCR**: POST `/realms/dcr/register` JSON {client_name, redirect_uris, grant_types:["authorization_code","refresh_token"], response_types:["code"], token_endpoint_auth_method:"client_secret_post"}; optional `Authorization: Bearer <token>` to own it. → 201 {client_id, client_secret}.
- **CIMD**: client_id = public HTTPS URL of a hosted JSON doc: {client_id:"<same URL>", client_name, redirect_uris:["…/callback"], grant_types:["authorization_code"], response_types:["code"], token_endpoint_auth_method:"none"}. No secret. AS fetches it at authorize time.
- **JWT**: RS256, kid `iic3103-tarea1`, verify vs shared JWKS. Claims: iss(realm), sub(email UC), aud(resource), scope, client_id, email, student_id, iat/exp.
- **AS metadata discovery order**: `/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server{path}` → `{issuer}/.well-known/openid-configuration` → `{issuer}/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server`.
- One `redirect_uri` (`/callback`) serves login + all 3 MCP flows; disambiguate via `state`. Common errors: invalid_target (resource mismatch authorize vs token), redirect_uri not registered (char-exact), invalid_grant (code reused/PKCE fail).

Rubric weights: PRE 10%, DCR 20%, CIMD 20%, tools/list 20%, tools/call 10%, deploy 10%, login 10%. Deploy must stay live 2 weeks for grading. See [[tarea1-plan]].

isolation.description: Isolation mode. "worktree" creates a temporary git worktree so the agent works on an isolated copy of the repo. "remote" launches the agent in a remote cloud environment (always runs in background; availability is gated).

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ReportFindings
tools.description: Report code-review findings as a typed list so the host UI can render them. Use this only when the active code-review instructions tell you to report findings with this tool; otherwise follow whatever output format those instructions specify. tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

tools.description:
Writes a file to the local filesystem, overwriting if one exists.

When to use: creating a new file, or fully replacing one you've already Read. Overwriting an existing file you haven't Read will fail. For partial changes, use Edit instead.

content.text:
**Recomendación: hazla sobre este código, pero entrégala en un repo nuevo.**

## Por qué conviene partir de este código

La Tarea 2 es una extensión de la Tarea 1. El enunciado pide mantener el login y las tres conexiones MCP en una vista de "Configuración" y agregar el chat encima. Casi todo lo que necesitas ya está en este repo:

- **Backend propio:** el enunciado exige un backend porque el navegador no puede hablar gRPC. Tu app Next.js ya ejecuta código en el servidor, así que `@grpc/grpc-js` y `@grpc/proto-loader` van en un Route Handler sin cambiar la arquitectura.
- **Conexiones MCP:** `src/lib/mcp/client.ts` ya tiene `tools/list` y `tools/call` con renovación de tokens. El loop del agente reutiliza eso directamente.
- **Base de datos:** Drizzle + Postgres ya está configurado. Solo hay que agregar tablas como `chats`, `messages` y `tool_calls`.
- **Login y aislamiento por usuario:** ya funcionan, y el historial de chats tiene que ser por usuario.

Partir de cero sería rehacer el 50–60% del trabajo.

## Por qué entregarla en otro repo

1. **El enunciado exige un repo nuevo:** la entrega va en el repo privado de GitHub Classroom que entrega el equipo docente para esta tarea. Lo práctico es trabajar aquí en una rama (o copiar el historial) y después hacer push a ese repo como un remote nuevo.
2. **No arriesgar el despliegue de la Tarea 1:** esa tarea debía quedar desplegada durante el periodo de corrección. Si modificas ese mismo servicio en Render, podrías romper algo que todavía están evaluando. Te recomiendo un servicio de Render aparte para la Tarea 2 (y una base de datos o schema aparte). Si cambia la URL, tienes que:
   - Agregar `<nueva-url>/callback` como redirect_uri del cliente PRE en `/console`.
   - Revisar que el documento CIMD (`/oauth/client-metadata.json`) apunte al nuevo dominio. Se genera a partir de `APP_BASE_URL`, así que debería ajustarse solo.

## Ojo con la fecha

Según el enunciado, la entrega es el **viernes 2 de octubre a las 18:00**, y hoy es 2 de octubre. Cada hora de atraso descuenta 0,2 puntos. Si esa fecha es correcta, el tiempo es muy justo. Confirma en Canvas si se cambió la fecha (el documento es la versión 1, del 6/09).

## Otros requisitos del enunciado

- Hay que versionar en el repo **todas las conversaciones con el agente de IA**.
- **No se permite usar IA para el documento de arquitectura.** El informe de aprendizajes es tuyo; te recomiendo escribirlo tú.
- Está prohibido usar LangChain u otros frameworks de agentes, y mandar tokens MCP al LLM. El loop se programa a mano.
- Ante `RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED` (rate limit), hay que mostrar el error sin reintentar en el backend.

Si quieres, armo el plan e implemento: proxy gRPC, loop del agente con máximo 12 turnos y nombres de tools con prefijo (`pre_`, `dcr_`, `cimd_`), tablas de chat, vista de chat con markdown sanitizado y la traza de cada tool, y Configuración como sección aparte. ¿Ya tienes el link del repo de Classroom?

# Render Blueprint. Deploy: New → Blueprint → point at this repo.
# Set the `sync: false` secrets in the Render dashboard after the first deploy.
services:
  - type: web
    name: integratrip-mcp-client
    runtime: node
    plan: free
    buildCommand: npm ci && npm run build
    # Apply DB migrations (idempotent) before starting the server.
    startCommand: npm run db:migrate && npm run start
    healthCheckPath: /api/health
    envVars:
      - key: NODE_VERSION
        value: "22"
      - key: AS_BASE_URL
        value: https://tarea1-auth-z2fqxmm2ja-uc.a.run.app
      - key: APP_LOGIN_REALM
        value: pre
      # Set APP_BASE_URL to the service's public URL, e.g.
      # https://integratrip-mcp-client.onrender.com
      - key: APP_BASE_URL
        sync: false
      - key: DATABASE_URL
        sync: false
      - key: ENCRYPTION_KEY
        sync: false
      - key: SESSION_SECRET
        sync: false
      - key: PRE_CLIENT_ID
        sync: false
      - key: PRE_CLIENT_SECRET
        sync: false

# ── IntegraTrip — variables de entorno ─────────────────────────────────────
# Copia este archivo a .env.local (desarrollo) y configura los valores en tu
# plataforma de despliegue. NUNCA subas .env.local ni secretos reales a Git.

# Origin público de ESTA app (sin slash final).
# Debe coincidir con el origin del redirect_uri registrado en el AS.
#   Local:      http://localhost:3000
#   Producción: https://<tu-servicio>.onrender.com
APP_BASE_URL=http://localhost:3000

# Servidor de Autenticación del curso (por defecto ya apunta al correcto).
AS_BASE_URL=https://tarea1-auth-z2fqxmm2ja-uc.a.run.app

# Realm usado para el login de la app (según docs del AS: pre).
APP_LOGIN_REALM=pre

# Postgres (Supabase). Usa la connection string del pooler.
DATABASE_URL=[REDACTED]host:5432/postgres

# Clave AES-256-GCM para cifrar secretos/tokens en la BD. 32 bytes en base64.
#   Genera una con:  node -e "console.log(require('crypto').randomBytes(32).toString('base64'))"
ENCRYPTION_KEY=

# Secreto para firmar la cookie de sesión (HMAC). >= 16 caracteres.
#   Genera uno con:  node -e "console.log(require('crypto').randomBytes(32).toString('base64url'))"
SESSION_SECRET=

# Cliente pre-registrado creado en el /console del AS (realm pre).
# Se usa para el login de la app Y para conectar Andes Air (PRE).
# Registra en el /console el redirect_uri: <APP_BASE_URL>/callback
PRE_CLIENT_ID=

content.thinking:
The local env file seems to be missing the PRE_CLIENT credentials, so those aren't configured locally — APP_BASE_URL is probably pointing to localhost, and DATABASE_URL looks like it's connecting to the same production Supabase DB from before. I need to be careful that adding new tables to that database stays purely additive.

I also need the student's email and ID for the LLM piece, so I should ask the user instead of guessing — I'll use their UC-issued email rather than a personal one since the course list requires it.

For architecture, I'm planning an `src/lib/llm/` module with a vendored proto file, a lazy-loaded gRPC client wrapper that maps errors into a typed `LlmError`, plus a catalog builder in `src/lib/agent/catalog.ts` that lists tools per connection, prefixes them by auth type, dedupes conflicting connections, and sanitizes names.

Now I'm thinking through `src/lib/agent/loop.ts`: it should load chat history, append the user's message, loop through tool calls up to 12 times, and persist each model/tool message as it happens. The tricky part is handling a RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED error mid-loop — I need to make sure any tool calls that already executed (like a booking) get recorded even if the LLM call fails afterward, so I'm leaning toward persisting everything as it happens and only marking failures separately rather than risking data loss or duplicate consecutive user turns.

To preserve proper alternation when converting stored history into LLM messages, I'll insert a synthetic MODEL text whenever a run ends in an error — storing an "error" role row that gets converted into a MODEL message like "[System error: ...]" when rebuilding the conversation for Gemini, regardless of whether it follows a USER or TOOL message.

I'm also planning the DB schema: chats with id/userId/title/timestamps, chat_messages with role enum (user/model/tool/error), text, functionCalls/functionResults as jsonb, and meta for model/usage/latency, plus a tool_invocations table linking tool calls to their requesting message with arguments, results, and duration for logging purposes.

I decide against encrypting stored history since tool results like booking IDs aren't sensitive secrets. For function result payloads, I'll prefer structuredContent if the MCP callTool result provides it, otherwise parse text content as JSON or fall back to a plain content wrapper, truncating to roughly 20k characters to avoid size errors. I also need to make sure access tokens are never sent to Gemini, and that MCP input schemas are sanitized since Gemini may reject certain JSON Schema features.

I realize I can't actually test against the proxy without credentials, since calls will fail with UNAUTHENTICATED until I have a UC email and student ID. I'm weighing whether to hardcode these in env vars as the assignment allows, or instead pull them from the logged-in user's session so each user consumes their own quota -- though that only works if their email is on the course's allowed list.

I'll go with env vars as primary, falling back to session values if unset, since that matches the assignment's suggestion while still being flexible for graders using their own accounts.

Since the proto has no system role, I also need to figure out how to inject instructions -- likely by prepending a synthetic user message with the instructions on every request, since nothing persists between calls.

The instructions themselves should cover: acting as a travel planner, collecting origin/destination/dates/passengers, using tools to search, presenting options, requiring explicit confirmation before booking flights or hotels, producing a final itinerary with confirmation IDs, including today's date, replying in the user's language, and formatting in markdown. I'll prepend this as a "[Instrucciones del sistema]" user turn followed by a "Entendido." model acknowledgment, then the real conversation history -- the extra token cost should be negligible.

For rate limiting, 12 calls per 60 seconds per student could realistically be hit in a longer conversation; I don't think there's much to do beyond surfacing the error cleanly rather than retrying automatically.

Now I'm sketching the UI structure -- routes for `/chat` as the chat list/new chat view and `/chat/[id]` for individual conversations, with a full-screen layout including a sidebar for the chat list and a "new chat" button.

Thinking through top navigation between Chat and Configuración, I'm debating whether to keep the existing `/dashboard` route relabeled as Configuración or rename it to `/settings`, and need to check where the login callback currently redirects so I don't break that flow -- post-login should land on `/chat`.

For the actual chat mechanics, I'm considering whether message creation should run synchronously (POST to create a chat, then POST messages that run the full tool-calling loop and return results) versus streaming — since a 12-turn loop with tool calls could take significant time, streaming NDJSON events for each step (tool call started/finished, text chunks) would give a much better live experience, and persistence should happen server-side regardless of whether the client disconnects mid-stream.

Given deadline pressure I weigh a simpler synchronous "pensando..." response against proper streaming, but since visualization quality matters I'm leaning toward implementing NDJSON streaming since it isn't too complex. For new chats I'm planning to create them lazily on first message via a single endpoint that accepts an optional chatId and creates one if missing, titling it from the first part of the message, then streaming a chat-id event the client uses to update the URL without remounting the component, refreshing the sidebar once the stream ends. For rendering, I'll use react-markdown with remark-gfm since it's safe by default (no raw HTML unless rehype-raw is added), satisfying the sanitized markdown requirement, and I'm thinking about whether to pull in the Tailwind typography plugin or just write small custom styled components.

I want each tool call in the thread shown as a collapsible card with the server badge, tool name, args, and result or error as JSON. For the tools catalog, I'll expose it via an API endpoint and cache it in memory per user for about two minutes since building it requires listing tools across multiple MCP connections per message, which is costly to redo constantly. If a connection fails (expired token, refresh failure) I want to skip that server's tools, add a warning note, and stream catalog warnings rather than failing the whole chat. I also need to inject today's date in the system prompt using the Chile timezone, and I'm now considering how proto-loader will resolve paths for loading the protobuf definitions in the Next.js environment.

I'm resolving the proto file path using the working directory, which should work fine on Render since the app starts from the repo root. Since grpc-js is pure JS it should bundle fine, but to be safe I'll mark it and proto-loader as external server packages. I'm also planning a script to export AI conversation logs for documentation, but I need to be careful since those conversations may contain secrets that were shared with the user, so the script should redact known env values before copying anything.

Now I still need to quickly check the remaining files — the callback route, ToolsPanel, ConnectForm, LogoutButton, the CI workflow, and the size of docs/architecture.md — plus look at the Next.js docs folder for anything relevant.

I also need to figure out how UI messages map to serialized ChatMessage rows and how tool invocations get paired with model function calls by id, deciding to store server info in the TOOL message's meta rather than polluting the stored LLM payloads. Then I'm working out how to convert history rows back into LlmMessage format for each role (user, model, tool).

For error handling, I'm reasoning that error rows always surface as a MODEL message with an apology text, and since tool execution failures are captured as is_error results rather than thrown errors, the error path only really applies around Generate calls, so the message sequence stays consistent without edge cases like back-to-back USER rows.

I'm also considering function call id quirks — if Gemini returns an empty id I'll generate one like `call_${n}` and make sure both the MODEL function call and the TOOL result use the same generated id so everything stays consistent when sent back through the proxy.

For MCP tool results, I'm deciding how to normalize them for the LLM: use structuredContent when available, otherwise concatenate text content and try parsing it as JSON, falling back to a plain text wrapper, and wrapping arrays or errors into object shapes; I'll also truncate overly large JSON payloads to 30k characters with a truncation flag. I'm planning to store the raw MCP result for the UI while storing the LLM-facing payload separately in functionResults, and to run multiple tool calls sequentially (safer for bookings) rather than in parallel, with a hard cap of 12 turns that produces an explicit "max turns reached" error row if no final text is returned.

Now I'm working out edge cases: an empty final response should render as "(sin respuesta)", identity resolution happens via resolveIdentity(session), and concurrent messages to the same chat need an in-memory lock per chatId to avoid sequence collisions, rejecting with 409 if a run is already active. content.thinking:
Now I'm planning the UI structure: a shared AppHeader with navigation across chat and dashboard pages, server-rendered chat routes that load chats and messages into a ChatView client component, and a layout with a sidebar for conversation list/creation plus a main thread area for messages and composer.

For message rendering I'm grouping rows by role—user messages as right-aligned bubbles, model text as markdown bubbles, and model function calls paired with their results from subsequent tool rows via id matching, with pending calls showing a loading state while streaming. I'm also adding an optional toggleable panel showing available tools with their schemas, using react-markdown with remark-gfm for formatting and a full-height flex layout for the page.

For client state, I'm defining a shared UiMessage type for serialized chat messages (dates as strings) and building the send flow: posting to the chat API, reading the streamed response line by line, and dispatching updates for new chat IDs, incoming messages, status changes, catalog info, and errors as each event type arrives.

On completion I decide against calling router.refresh() since ChatView's state is only initialized from props on mount — instead I'll keep the chats list in client state and just reorder it locally when a new message arrives. I'm also thinking about making sending feel instant by clearing the input and showing a sending indicator right away, and handling chat navigation by keying ChatView on chatId so switching conversations resets state properly.

There's a wrinkle though: since I used replaceState to update the URL to /chat/id, Next's router might think we're already on that route, so clicking "Nueva conversación" linking to /chat could be a no-op if the pathname doesn't actually change. To handle this safely, I'll have the button both push to /chat and manually reset local state (clearing messages and chatId) so it works regardless of whether Next's router syncing catches the pathname change.

For the sidebar, deleting a conversation removes it from the list via DELETE fetch, and resets to a new chat if it was the active one. The catalog drawer fetches data on open, mobile just hides the sidebar below md breakpoint with a simple toggle, and I'll add a server-rendered AppHeader component with nav links. The landing page redirects to /chat if there's a session, login callback also redirects to /chat, and the dashboard gets the title "Configuración".

Now I'm ready to start writing the actual files.

content.text:
Dejé la Tarea 2 construida sobre el código de la Tarea 1, en este mismo workspace. Compila, pasa lint y el build. **Todavía no la probé contra el LLM real** porque me faltan tus credenciales del proxy. Nada está commiteado ni pusheado.

## ¿Otro repo o este?

- **El código parte de aquí:** la Tarea 2 extiende la Tarea 1, así que lo construí encima de lo que ya tenías.
- **La entrega va en otro repo, privado:** tu repo `integratrip-mcp-client` es **público**, y el enunciado pide uno privado. Si subes ahí la Tarea 2, otros pueden copiarla. Busqué en tu GitHub y todavía no existe un repo de Classroom de IIC3103. Mientras no te lo den, creamos uno privado tuyo y después lo pasamos al de Classroom.
- **Despliegue aparte:** conviene un servicio de Render nuevo (`integratrip-tarea2`) para no romper el de la Tarea 1 mientras lo corrigen.

## Lo que quedó hecho

- **Cliente gRPC del LLM:** usa el `.proto` del curso, copiado en `proto/llm.proto`, y manda tu email y número de alumno en cada llamada. Probé el canal con credenciales falsas y respondió `PERMISSION_DENIED`, así que la conexión funciona.
- **Catálogo de tools:** junta las tools de tus MCP conectados con prefijo por servidor (`pre_*`, `dcr_*`, `cimd_*`) y se puede ver desde el botón "🔧 Tools" del chat.
- **Loop del agente:** máximo 12 turnos; ejecuta todas las tools que pide el modelo antes del siguiente `Generate`, y guarda cada paso en la base de datos.
- **Instrucciones al agente:** pedir los datos que falten, no inventar nada y pedir confirmación explícita antes de reservar vuelo u hotel.
- **Rate limit:** si el proxy responde `RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED`, el backend no reintenta; muestra el aviso y el usuario reenvía su mensaje.
- **Base de datos:** tres tablas nuevas, `chats`, `chat_messages` y `tool_invocations`, en la migración `drizzle/0001_chats.sql`. Al retomar un chat se reconstruye el mismo contexto; una conversación nueva parte vacía.
- **Vista de chat a pantalla completa:** `/chat` y `/chat/[id]`, con lista de conversaciones, botón de nueva conversación, respuestas en markdown y una tarjeta por cada tool ejecutada (argumentos, resultado o error y duración). Las respuestas aparecen en vivo mientras el agente trabaja.
- **Configuración:** lo de la Tarea 1 quedó en `/dashboard` con la etiqueta "Configuración" y navegación entre Chat y Configuración. Después del login se entra directo al chat.
- **Conversaciones con IA:** el enunciado exige subirlas al repo. `node scripts/export-ai-conversations.mjs` las copia a `ai-conversations/` y censura los secretos. Revisa el resultado antes de commitear: la conversación de la Tarea 1 tenía secretos.
- **Documentación:** actualicé el README, `.env.example` y `render.yaml`.

## Lo que necesito de ti

1. **Tu email UC y número de alumno** para el proxy del LLM. Con eso pruebo el agente de punta a punta.
2. **Base de datos:** ¿creo las tablas en tu Supabase actual o creas uno nuevo para la Tarea 2? No apliqué la migración en ninguna base.
3. **Repo:** ¿te creo ahora un repo privado `integratrip-tarea2` en tu GitHub y hago commit y push ahí? ¿O ya tienes el link de Classroom?
4. **Render:** cuando exista el servicio nuevo, agrega `<nueva-url>/callback` como redirect_uri en el `/console` del AS y configura `LLM_STUDENT_EMAIL` y `LLM_STUDENT_ID`.

Hay dos cosas que tienes que escribir tú porque el enunciado prohíbe usar IA para el documento de arquitectura: actualizar `docs/architecture.md` y el informe de aprendizajes. Por consistencia, te sugiero escribir el informe a mano también.

**Ojo con la fecha:** el enunciado dice viernes 2 de octubre a las 18:00, que es hoy, y cada hora de atraso descuenta 0,2 puntos. Si nadie la cambió en Canvas, lo más urgente es tener las credenciales del LLM y el deploy.

Te corrijo dos cosas que dije antes y te cuento cómo vamos.

## ¿Dónde dice lo del repo privado?

En la página 9, sección "Versionamiento de código":

> "Todo el código de su servicio deberá estar versionado en un **repositorio privado que será provisto por el equipo docente**. Para desarrollar puedes trabajar en un repositorio propio mientras no hayamos dado acceso al repositorio final."

En "Requisitos mínimos" (página 10) agrega: "El código deberá estar versionado en su totalidad en el repositorio de GitHub Classroom de esta tarea."

**Exageré en un punto:** el enunciado no prohíbe que tu repo personal sea público. Solo exige que la entrega final esté en el repo privado de Classroom. Lo de "otros pueden copiarla" fue inferencia mía, no lo dice el enunciado. Aun así, con código público, si alguien copia, los dos quedan expuestos a la sanción por integridad académica. Por eso te recomiendo un repo privado para desarrollar, aunque no sea obligatorio.

## El LLM ya funciona con tus credenciales

- Responde con `gemini-2.5-flash-lite`.
- Probé también el ciclo completo con una tool: el modelo pide la tool, se ejecuta, se le manda el resultado y responde.
- Encontré un problema del proxy: **a veces** devuelve `INTERNAL: Gemini returned an empty response` justo después de un resultado de tool. Pasó en 4 de 8 intentos, con cualquier formato de mensaje, así que no es un error nuestro.
- Le puse **un solo reintento** a ese caso. `RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED` se sigue mostrando al usuario sin reintentar, como pide el enunciado.
- Guardé tu email y número de alumno en `.env.local`, que no se sube a git.

## Render: sí, lo puedo operar yo

El CLI de Render no sirve para esto: no crea servicios nuevos y su login necesita que apruebes en el navegador. Lo hago con la **API de Render**, que permite crear el servicio, configurar las variables, hacer deploy y ver los logs. Necesito:

1. **Una API key de Render**: Dashboard → Account Settings → API Keys → Create. **No me la pegues en el chat.** Las conversaciones se van a subir al repo; el script de exportación censura lo que está en `.env.local`, pero no lo que escribes en el chat. Agrégala tú en una línea de `.env.local`:
   ```
   RENDER_API_KEY=rnd_...
   ```
2. **El repo:** ¿creo `mtombolini/integratrip-tarea2` privado en tu GitHub y subo el código? Render tiene que poder leer ese repo. Si su app de GitHub está limitada a repos específicos, tendrás que agregarlo en GitHub → Settings → Applications → Render.
3. **La base de datos, tienes que elegir:**
   - **(a) Usar el mismo Supabase de `.env.local`:** solo agrega tablas nuevas, no toca las de la Tarea 1. Es lo más rápido.
   - **(b) Crear un proyecto Supabase nuevo:** lo creas tú y pegas la URL en `.env.local` como `DATABASE_URL_T2`.

   Ojo: Supabase gratis pausa los proyectos tras 7 días sin actividad, y eso podría pillarte durante la corrección.

Con la API key en `.env.local` y tus respuestas a 2 y 3, hago el deploy. Después solo te queda agregar `https://<nueva-url>/callback` como redirect_uri del cliente PRE en el `/console` del AS, porque eso no se puede hacer por API.

  - `/api/health` responde ok.
  - El documento CIMD ya usa el dominio nuevo.
  - `/chat` sin sesión redirige al inicio.
- **Configuración del servicio nuevo:**
  - Comparte con la Tarea 1 la base Supabase, la clave de cifrado y el cliente PRE, así que las conexiones guardadas sirven en ambos deploys.
  - Tiene su propio secreto de sesión y tus credenciales del LLM.
- **Supabase:** la migración se aplicó al arrancar el servicio. Agregó las tablas `chats`, `chat_messages` y `tool_invocations`; las de la Tarea 1 no se tocaron.

## Lo que falta de tu parte

1. **Registrar el redirect_uri (bloqueante).** Lo probé y hoy el AS responde `redirect_uri not registered for client`. En el `/console` del AS, en tu cliente `[REDACTED]`, agrega:
   ```
   https://integratrip-tarea2.onrender.com/callback
   ```
   Deja también el de la Tarea 1. Con eso funcionan el login y la conexión con Andes Air. StayWell y Cielo Sur no necesitan nada: se registran solos con la URL nueva.
2. **Rotar la API key de Render.** Quedó escrita en el chat, y las conversaciones se van a subir al repo. Crea una nueva en Render (Account Settings → API Keys), borra la anterior y reemplázala en `.env.local`. El script de exportación ya censura cualquier key `rnd_…`, pero rotarla es lo seguro.

content.text:
Se hace en la consola del servidor de autenticación del curso (el AS). La URL la verifiqué: te pide iniciar sesión primero.

## Pasos

1. Abre **https://tarea1-auth-z2fqxmm2ja-uc.a.run.app/console**
2. Inicia sesión con tu email UC (`[REDACTED]`) y tu número de alumno como contraseña.
3. Busca tu cliente con client_id **`[REDACTED]`**. Es el que creaste para la Tarea 1 y debería tener registrado `https://integratrip-mcp-client.onrender.com/callback`.
4. En sus redirect URIs **agrega** esta línea y deja la de la Tarea 1:
   ```
   https://integratrip-tarea2.onrender.com/callback
   ```
   Tiene que quedar exacta: con `https`, sin slash al final.
5. Guarda.

## Si la consola no deja editar el cliente

No pude ver la consola por dentro sin tu sesión, así que no sé si permite editar un cliente existente. Si no lo permite:

1. Crea un **cliente nuevo** con las dos redirect URIs (la de la Tarea 1 y la nueva).
2. Pásame el nuevo client_id y secret de la misma forma que la API key: en `.env.local`, como `PRE_CLIENT_ID_T2` y `PRE_CLIENT_SECRET_T2`, no en el chat.
3. Yo los configuro en el servicio de Render de la Tarea 2 y redespliego. El deploy de la Tarea 1 sigue usando su cliente actual.

## Cuando termines

Avísame y verifico que el AS acepte la URL nueva. Después:

1. Entra a https://integratrip-tarea2.onrender.com
2. Conecta los 3 MCP en **Configuración**.
3. Prueba un viaje completo en **Chat**. Mientras pruebas, yo reviso los logs de Render.

Lo de rotar la API key queda para después, anotado.

content.thinking:
I'm planning the app shell layout: a single unified left sidebar merging navigation (Chat, Configuración) with the conversation list, similar to ChatGPT's structure, topped with the IntegraTrip logo.

For syncing the chat list when a new conversation starts, I'm weighing a client-side context provider (`ChatsProvider`) that holds the chats array, seeded from the server and updated optimistically by ChatView when it creates a new chat, versus relying on `router.refresh()` after the chat is saved -- the context approach avoids the remount flash that refreshing would cause mid-stream.

I'm also planning the route group restructuring: moving chat and dashboard routes under `app/(app)/...` with a shared layout that handles auth redirect, loads chats, and wraps everything in the sidebar plus a scrollable main area, with mobile handled via a top bar and drawer in the Sidebar component. For the Configuración page redesign, I'm sketching a header, a "Servidores MCP" section with preset cards for each integration showing connection status and action buttons, plus an "Otras conexiones" list for custom non-preset URLs.

I'm figuring out the connection detail page should stay but fit inside the new shell with a back link, and the ConnectForm should split into a server-rendered ServerCard and an advanced client-side CustomConnectForm, keeping the existing delete button's label. For ChatView, I'm removing its internal sidebar in favor of the shared context, keeping the catalog panel and thread view, and moving the mobile conversation list into the app-level sidebar drawer -- with the Sidebar tracking the active route and current chat id via the pathname.

I'm realizing there's a subtle bug: after a route replace to /chat/[id], navigating back to /chat with "Nueva conversación" could reuse the same ChatView instance and preserve stale messages since the key doesn't change. I'm fixing this by having the context expose a reset signal that ChatView watches via an effect to clear its state whenever a new chat is requested or a chat is deleted, combined with a router.push to /chat.

Now I'll write the ChatsContext file, making sure chat titles shown in the ChatView header pull from this shared context, then move on to writing out all the remaining files.

El enunciado de la Tarea 2 **no define un documento de arquitectura**. Lo único que lo menciona es una línea de la sección "Uso de IA" (página 10):

> "No se permite el uso de IA en la generación del documento de arquitectura de solución requerido en esta tarea."

No aparece en otra parte del enunciado:
- **Entregables (página 9):** solo URL del servicio desplegado, documento de aprendizajes y URL del repo en GitHub.
- **Rúbrica (página 12):** no tiene un ítem de arquitectura.
- **Contenido:** ninguna sección dice qué debería contener.

Esa frase parece heredada del enunciado de la Tarea 1. Te recomiendo preguntar en el foro o a los ayudantes si se pide para esta tarea.

## Lo que sí se pide: Informe de aprendizajes (10% de la nota)

Según la página 8, es un informe de reflexión sobre la **Tarea 1 y la Tarea 2** que debe comentar, entre otros aspectos:
- Qué aprendiste durante el desarrollo del proyecto.
- Qué aspectos de la tarea te gustaron y cuáles no.
- Qué dificultades encontraste y cómo las resolviste.
- Qué conceptos o tecnologías te resultaron más interesantes.
- Cualquier otro comentario, opinión o aprendizaje sobre la experiencia.

El enunciado insiste en que sea **reflexión sobre la experiencia, no una descripción de lo implementado**. No prohíbe usar IA para este informe, pero como es personal conviene que lo escribas tú.

## Si igual quieres actualizar la arquitectura (opción segura)

Ya tienes `docs/architecture.md` de la Tarea 1. Para que cubra la Tarea 2, tendrías que agregarle, con tus palabras:
1. **Componentes nuevos:** cliente gRPC al proxy LLM (con metadata `x-student-email` y `x-student-id`), catálogo de tools con prefijos (`pre_`, `dcr_`, `cimd_`), loop del agente y la API de chat.
2. **Modelo entidad-relación extendido:** tablas `chats`, `chat_messages` (roles user, model, tool y error, ordenados por `seq`) y `tool_invocations`, y cómo se relacionan con `users` y `mcp_connections`.
3. **Diagrama de secuencia del loop:** usuario → API → `Generate` → `function_calls` → `tools/call` en el MCP correcto → `Generate`, hasta el texto final o 12 turnos.
4. **Manejo del contexto:** cómo retomar un chat reconstruye el historial USER/MODEL/TOOL, y que una conversación nueva parte vacía.
5. **Errores y límites:** `RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED` sin reintento en el backend, el reintento único ante `INTERNAL` y el máximo de 12 turnos.
6. **Seguridad:** los tokens de los MCP nunca se mandan a `Generate`, y el markdown se renderiza sin HTML crudo.

Como es el documento donde no se permite IA, no lo redacto yo. Lo que sí puedo hacer es revisarlo después contra el código, para confirmar que lo que describas sea correcto.

**Algo que encontré revisando:** el primer commit de la Tarea 2 incluyó un cambio de una línea en `docs/architecture.md`, en el diagrama de login: "redirect /dashboard" pasó a "redirect /chat". Yo no lo edité a propósito; apareció modificado durante la sesión y entró en mi commit. El cambio es correcto, pero dada esa regla, ¿lo revierto para que lo hagas tú a mano?

content.text:
Sí, en casi todo, pero hay dos criterios con riesgo y uno que depende de ti.

| Criterio | Estado | Evidencia |
|---|---|---|
| **Despliegue de app** (1) | ✅ Cumple | En vivo en `integratrip-tarea2.onrender.com`, se despliega desde tu repo y migró la base sola. ⚠️ Riesgo: Supabase gratis pausa la base tras 7 días sin uso, y la corrección dura 2 semanas. |
| **Informe de aprendizajes** (1) | ⏳ Pendiente | Lo escribes tú. |
| **Vista de chats** (1) | ✅ Cumple | Chat a pantalla completa, separado de Configuración, con sidebar. Permite nueva conversación, ver la lista y retomar chats anteriores. |
| **Loop de agente** (2) | ✅ Cumple | Máximo 12 turnos y nombres con prefijo (`pre_`, `dcr_`, `cimd_`). Ejecuta todas las tools en el MCP correcto antes del siguiente `Generate`. Ante `RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED` no reintenta. En tu prueba hizo 3 reservas en un mismo turno. |
| **Manejo de contexto entre conversaciones** (2) | ✅ Cumple | Las respuestas de seguimiento usan el historial completo: tu "La confirmo" reservó lo acordado varios mensajes antes. Al retomar un chat se reconstruye desde la base, y una conversación nueva parte vacía. Cada usuario solo ve sus chats. |
| **Visualización de mensajes y tools** (1) | 🟡 Probable, con riesgo | El markdown se ve bien y cada tool muestra nombre, servidor, estado y duración. Pero **los argumentos y el resultado solo aparecen al hacer clic** en la tarjeta. El enunciado pide una "traza visible de cada tool (nombre, argumentos, resultado o error)", y un corrector estricto podría no expandirla. |
| **Respuestas con sentido y objetivo logrado** (2) | 🟡 Probable, con riesgo | El objetivo se logró: reservó vuelo y hotel y entregó los IDs. Pero en tu prueba vi tres cosas: **no incluyó el clima** en el resumen final (el ejemplo del enunciado sí lo incluye), **preguntó el año** sin necesidad y una respuesta salió rara ("SantiagodeChile o SCL"). |

## Lo que propongo ajustar (unos 15 minutos)

1. **Tarjetas de tool:** mostrar los argumentos resumidos sin necesidad de hacer clic, por ejemplo `origin=SCL · destination=CUN · date=2026-08-31`. El resultado completo seguiría al expandir.
2. **Instrucciones del agente:**
   - Consultar siempre el clima del destino e incluirlo en el resumen final, junto con los IDs.
   - Asumir el año sin preguntarlo cuando no se indica.
   - Agrupar en un solo mensaje las preguntas por datos que falten.
3. **GitHub Action contra la pausa de Supabase:** una consulta a la base cada 3 días, para que el servicio siga funcionando durante la corrección.

Después vuelvo a probar un viaje completo en producción y te muestro el resultado. ¿Lo hago?

## ¿Por qué NO backend separado?

No es que esté prohibido — el enunciado lo permite explícitamente. Es una decisión de **costo/beneficio** para tu situación (solo, con deadline apretado):

| | Monolito (Next.js) | Backend + Frontend separados |
|---|---|---|
| **Despliegues** | 1 servicio | 2 servicios (2 URLs, 2 configs, 2 cold starts) |
| **CORS** | No existe (mismo origen) | Hay que configurarlo y sufrirlo |
| **Cookies httpOnly de sesión** | Triviales (mismo dominio) | Complicado cross-domain (SameSite, dominios) |
| **redirect_uri de OAuth** | Una sola URL estable | Coordinar entre front y back |

| **Tiempo hasta desplegar** | Menor | Mayor |

El enunciado dice literalmente que **no evalúa la arquitectura específica**, sino que esté "correctamente diseñada, sea mantenible y permita evolución". El monolito Next.js **sí cumple separación de responsabilidades** — la separas por *capas* (`lib/oauth`, `lib/mcp`, `lib/db`, `components`), no por *procesos*. Obtienes la misma limpieza con la mitad de fricción operacional.

**Importante:** aunque sea un solo servicio, la comunicación con los MCP y el manejo de credenciales ocurre en los **Route Handlers / Server Components** (server-side). El navegador nunca ve un secreto. Cumple la seguridad igual que un backend separado.
